newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin replaces Lebed with loyal moderate.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin replaces Lebed with loyal moderate.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, in a surprise move, on Saturday named a loyal moderate, Ivan Rybkin, to replace controversial retired general Alexander Lebed as his security supremo.
Yeltsin appointed Rybkin, former speaker of the State Duma lower house of parliament, as secretary of his powerful Security Council and his personal envoy to breakaway Chechnya.

Yeltsin dramatically sacked Lebed on Thursday, accusing him of lack of team spirit and naked presidential ambitions. On Saturday he dismissed him as his representative in the breakaway region of Chechnya.
In a short meeting, filmed by Yeltsin's press service, the president told Rybkin: "I am sure you will succeed. Good luck."
The meeting took place in the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow where the 65-year-old Kremlin leader is preparing for heart surgery, expected in mid-November.
Lebed reacted in typically scornful manner, dismissing Rybkin as an incompetent bureaucrat.
Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as saying Rybkin was "unable to ensure the security of the country at a time when there are many dangers facing it".
Under Rybkin, the Security Council would "turn into a quiet bureaucratic office that no one will know about," Lebed said.
The Kremlin press service said Yeltsin urged Rybkin to work in close cooperation with all branches of power in Russia.
Lebed, in his four months in office, antagonised much of the Russian establishment with his unconcealed presidential ambitions and unwillingness to play by the Kremlin rules.
But his already high popularity was boosted further by an August peace deal with Chechen separatists, which ended 21 months of bloody war in which tens of thousands have died.
The Chechens have warned that Lebed's dismissal could lead to a deterioration of the situation there. There was no immediate reaction from them over Rybkin's appointment.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin told Rybkin to preserve the pace of the peace settlement in Chechnya.
"I am a convinced supporter of peace agreements in Chechnya and will do everything to get out of the crisis," Rybkin told RIA news agency.
Rybkin, who turns 50 on Sunday, is unlikely to stir trouble in the Kremlin or to try to assume a dominant public image while Yeltsin is ill.
He was elected to the Duma in 1993 as a member of the conservative Agrarian Party, allied to the communists, but broke with the party after becoming parliamentary speaker and a supporter of Yeltsin.

Exerting a moderate influence as speaker, Rybkin steered the Duma away from any clashes with the president. After the 1995 parliamentary election, he failed to win a second term because the communists and their allies voted against him.
"He (Rybkin) will behave like he did in his time at the Duma, when he would calmly continue speaking from his presiding chair while deputies were fighting in the hall," Lebed said.
Yeltsin's press secretary told Interfax the president was considering whether to scrap altogether the third post Lebed had held -- the president's national security adviser.
Lebed has made clear he will pursue his ambitions and some experts say his sacking will only boost his long-term chances of becoming the next Kremlin leader.
The former paratroop commander, his confidence apparently undimmed by his sudden dismissal, shows no signs of wanting to quit the limelight.

"Russia is the richest country in the world yet Russians are among the poorest people in the world. This cannot be right," Lebed declared on Friday, citing the social inequalities that could help him rebuild his political career.
"I shall take a rest, then I shall start to work," he told reporters with a broad smile, but gave no details.
